items.readable_text:
Content:
When we multiply a function by a constant, the graph either stretches out or compresses. Transforming a function in this way is called scaling.

Content:
To illustrate, consider the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] shown below.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/f7485248b3f5658e5bb5d3ded2eb4785]

Content:
The following table lists four sets of points. The set of points in the left-hand column correspond to the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] and the set on the right-hand side corresponds to [MATH: y=2f(x).]

Content:
[MATH: Points on [math]y=f(x)[/math]|Points on [math]y=2f(x)[/math]; (1, 2)|(1, 4); (4, − 3)|(4, − 6); (0, 2)|(0, 4); (− 2, 0)|(− 2, 0)]

Content:
For each point on the graph of [MATH: y=f(x),] there is a point on the graph of [MATH: y=2f(x)] with the same [MATH: x]-value and double the [MATH: y]-value.

Content:
Now that we have four points on the graph of [MATH: y=2f(x),] let's plot the full graph.

Graphic:
[IMG: /graphics/9b5840dcf6d1d828021ae25843ddd186]

Content:
We say that the graph of [MATH: y=2f(x)] is the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] vertically stretched by a scale factor of [MATH: 2.]

Content:
We can also say that the graph of [MATH: y=2f(x)] is the graph of [MATH: y=f(x)] stretched by a factor of [MATH: 2] parallel to the [MATH: \mathbf y]-axis.
